column3: The Hebrew repeats Jonathan’s identity as “son of Saul” in the second clause; BSB leaves this description implicit.
Close to the Hebrew.

The Hebrew says Jonathan will speak about David to his father; BSB makes this specifically asking about him. Jonathan then says he will see what happens, where BSB has an “if I find out anything” clause.
Close to the Hebrew.
The Hebrew says David placed his “soul in his palm,” both singular; BSB uses “life in his hands.”
The Hebrew repeats Saul’s name before his oath and leaves the person not to be killed unnamed; BSB omits the repeated Saul and supplies David.

The Hebrew names Jonathan three times and says David was before Saul “as yesterday, the day before yesterday.” BSB names Jonathan twice and renders the time expression as serving him “as he had before.”
Close to the Hebrew.
The Hebrew calls the spirit “evil” and explicitly names David’s playing hand without naming the instrument. BSB uses “a spirit of distress” and supplies “the harp.”
The Hebrew actively describes Saul driving the spear into the wall; BSB makes the spear itself the subject of striking the wall.
The Hebrew describes the threatened fate with passive “you are being put to death”; BSB states the result as “you will be dead.”
The Hebrew uses three verbs for going, fleeing, and escaping; BSB combines the first two as “ran away.”
The Hebrew uses the plural form “teraphim”; BSB has singular “a household idol.”
The Hebrew leaves the woman speaking unnamed; BSB identifies her as Michal.
The Hebrew has no separate word for “back” in Saul’s sending of the messengers.
The Hebrew again uses plural “teraphim”; BSB has singular “the idol.”
The Hebrew gives David’s threat as “Why should I kill you?”; BSB turns this into “or I will kill you!”
Close to the Hebrew.
Close to the Hebrew.
The Hebrew explicitly names Saul as the sender and David as the one to be seized; BSB uses pronouns. Samuel is described as standing over the prophets, rendered “leading them” in BSB.
The Hebrew actively says unnamed people told Saul; BSB uses passive “this was reported to Saul.”
The Hebrew leaves both the traveler and the answering speaker unnamed; BSB identifies the traveler as Saul and makes the reply passive “he was told.”
The Hebrew uses pronouns for Saul twice; BSB names him twice.
The Hebrew says he fell naked, with a time expression covering day and night; BSB supplies a separate “lay” verb and names Saul where the Hebrew uses a pronoun.
